title: The Answer Machine: Socrates on Thinking for Yourself
topic: relying on instant answers instead of thinking things through
excerpt: Socrates taught that wisdom begins with knowing what you do not know, and he warned that writing could give people the appearance of wisdom without the substance. In this imagined letter he answers a reader who asks a machine almost everything and finds they can no longer defend what they believe.

sections.text:
You write that you now ask a machine almost everything. What to cook, how to word a hard message to your sister, whether a pain in your side is worth a doctor, what a book you have not read is about. The answers come at once and they sound sure of themselves. And yet you tell me that you feel less certain of anything than you did a few years ago, and that when a friend pushed back on something you had said, you found you could not defend it, because you had never really thought it through. You only had the answer.

You ask an old man who wrote nothing down whether he has any advice. I have a little, and most of it comes in the form of questions, which you will have to forgive. That was always my way.

sections.heading: The Gift That Makes People Seem Wise
sections.text:
When I was in Athens, the new marvel was the written word. Books were spreading, and young men could buy the speeches of famous orators and carry them home. I once walked out past the city walls with a young friend named Phaedrus, who had a speech tucked under his cloak and was eager to learn it by heart. We sat under a plane tree by the river, and I told him a story about the Egyptian god who invented writing and brought it as a gift to the king.

The god promised that writing would make people wiser and improve their memory. The king disagreed. He said it would do the opposite. People would stop exercising their memory because they could trust the marks on the page. They would read a great deal without being taught, and so they would seem to know many things while knowing very little. They would be hard company, too, because they would have the appearance of wisdom without the substance.

I did not tell that story because I hated books. I told it because a written speech has a peculiar weakness. Ask it a question and it says the same thing again. It cannot explain what it meant, cannot notice that you have misunderstood, and cannot defend itself when someone attacks it. It needs its author standing by to help it, and the author is usually somewhere else.

Your machine is cleverer than a scroll. It will answer a follow up question, and it will rephrase itself as often as you like. I will grant it that. But notice what you described. You had an answer, and when your friend questioned it, the answer could not stand up, because the part that should have defended it, your own understanding, had never been built. The appearance of wisdom arrived and the wisdom did not.

sections.heading: What I Learned in the Agora
sections.text:
A friend of mine named Chaerephon once went to the oracle at Delphi and asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The priestess said no one was. This troubled me a great deal, because I knew I was not wise about anything important. So I set out to prove the god wrong by finding someone wiser than me.

I went first to the politicians, who were famous for their wisdom. When I questioned them, they could not say what justice was, though they spoke about it every day. I went to the poets, who wrote beautiful lines about courage and the gods but could not explain a word of what they had written. I went to the craftsmen, and they at least knew their trades, but because they were good at making shoes or pots they believed they understood everything else as well.

In the end I decided the oracle meant something modest. I was wiser than these men only in one small way. They thought they knew what they did not know, and I knew that I did not know. That small difference turned out to matter enormously.

Here is my worry for you. The machine gives you the answer before you have discovered that you did not know it. It skips the very moment that made me wiser than the politicians, the moment of being stuck, of saying honestly that you have no idea. That moment is uncomfortable, and so a device that spares you from it will feel like a kindness. I suspect it is the opposite of one.

sections.heading: Knowledge Has to Be Born
sections.text:
My mother was a midwife, and I used to say that I practised her trade on minds instead of bodies. I could not put an idea into anyone. What I could do was ask questions until the idea that was already forming in them came out, and then help them test whether it was healthy or only a wind egg, something that looked like a child and had nothing inside.

That process is slow and often embarrassing. A young man would offer me a definition of courage, I would ask about a case it did not fit, and he would have to start again. Sometimes we went round three or four times and ended the afternoon with no definition at all. Yet he went home knowing far more than when he came, because he now understood why the easy answers fail. The knowledge was his own. Nobody could take it from him by asking a hard question, because he had already asked himself the hard questions.

An answer handed to you is a different thing from an answer you have given birth to. One you can repeat. The other you can defend, change, and build on. When your friend pushed back, you discovered which kind you had been collecting.

sections.heading: A Small Practice
sections.text:
I will not tell you to throw the machine into the sea. I drank from the public fountains and walked on roads other men built, and when I was young I got hold of the books of Anaxagoras and read them as fast as I could, hoping they would tell me why things are as they are. The question is who does the thinking.

So try this. Before you ask the machine anything that matters to you, ask yourself first. Say out loud, or write if you must, what you already believe and why. Then notice where your reasons run out. That place, where you would have to say I do not know, is the most valuable thing you will find all day. Stay there a while before you go looking for help.

When you do ask, treat the answer the way I treated the confident men in the agora. Ask it what it means by its words. Look for a case it does not fit. Ask a friend to argue the other side. If the answer survives your questions, keep it, and it will finally be yours. If it collapses, you have lost nothing but a false belief, which is a good day's work.

And for the questions about how to live, how to speak to your sister, what you owe the people around you, what kind of person you are trying to become, I would not ask the machine at all. Those questions were never meant to be settled by someone else. They are settled by living them and examining the living, slowly, with people who care about you enough to disagree.

sections.heading: Why It Is Worth the Trouble
sections.text:
The Athenians eventually put me on trial. I told the jury that even if they offered to set me free on condition that I stop questioning people, I would refuse. I had come to believe that a life without this kind of examination was not worth living for a human being, and I meant it. I was seventy years old. I would not propose exile, and when my friends arranged an escape from prison I would not take it. I drank the hemlock instead.

I do not ask anything so dramatic of you. I ask only that you keep a small part of your mind for the slow work of not knowing, questioning, and finding out. The machine can carry a great many of your burdens. Let it. But the one burden it cannot carry for you is the one that makes you a thinking person, and that is the burden worth keeping.
